narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 71% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction to assess risk, your application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the strongest influences pushing the model toward predicting failure. Both placed you in the bottom decile of your school, far below the average of roughly the 6th decile among students who were accepted. These unusually low rankings signaled to the model a pattern of academic struggle that strongly suggested difficulty passing the bar.

Your undergraduate GPA was the third most important factor, but it worked in the opposite direction. At 3.10 it was only slightly below the 3.23 average of accepted students, so it mildly supported the chance you might pass. Unfortunately, this positive signal was not strong enough to outweigh the much larger negative impact of your class rankings.

The model also noted your LSAT score of 28, well below the 37 average of accepted applicants, and your plan to attend full-time, which is the norm for most successful candidates. However, these played smaller roles than your school performance.

You should focus on strengthening your academic foundation, perhaps by retaking key courses, seeking tutoring, or gaining additional legal experience before reapplying. Improving your class standing and test scores in a visible way would directly address the factors that led to this rejection. (248 words)
